If you can delete data/processed/, results/ and figures/, run one command and get them all back, the project is reproducible — and that single test is the one a reviewer effectively applies.

Bridge — where this template is used across the group’s courses

Unit 2 puts this layout under version control and adds the data manifest; Unit 3 fills data/raw/ from APIs and databases. The later units of this R edition are built in the same sequence as the Python edition, whose counterparts of this unit’s successors already exist: tidy data produces data/processed/, software engineering for scientists turns R/ into a tested, installable package, and the capstone is carried out on exactly this layout. The cheminformatics elective uses the same skeleton for molecular work — see its units on databases and curation — while BGM324 shows what the structural tools in molecular docking and molecular dynamics deposit into data/raw/, and the R edition of the AI course BGM411 (study material) uses the same R/ discipline for its model code.

8. Working with an AI coding assistant

AI coding assistants are part of the working environment, and pretending otherwise would make this unit obsolete on the day it was written. They are useful for the kind of code this course produces: a ggplot2 idiom you have forgotten, a tidyr reshape, a roxygen comment, a first draft of a function whose logic you already know. They are also, measurably, a source of defects — an audit of assistant-generated code found that a substantial share of security-relevant completions contained vulnerabilities[22], the underlying models pass functional-correctness benchmarks only partially[23], and in scientific work the characteristic failure is not a crash but a plausible wrong number[24]. Scientific publishing has converged on a simple position: the tool is not an author and the human is accountable for every line[25].

This group’s policy therefore has five steps, in order, and the middle three are not optional.

  1. Draft. Ask the assistant for a first version, with the context it needs (the column types, the lengths, the units).
  2. Read. Read every line. If you cannot say what a line does, delete it or learn it — there is no third option.
  3. Test. Write the check yourself, on a case whose answer you know independently (by hand, from a published value, or from a degenerate case).
  4. Explain. Be able to explain the code to your supervisor without the assistant open. If you cannot, you do not own it.
  5. Attribute. Record in the project README that an assistant was used and for what. This is the same courtesy as citing a package.

The next chunk shows why step 3 is the load-bearing one, using a draft that is wrong in the way assistants are characteristically wrong: fluent, well-formatted, documented, and off by a constant.

## Step 3 in action: a plausible 'assistant draft' and the four-line test that rejects it.
pactivity_draft <- function(value_nm) {
  # Convert a concentration to pActivity. (A plausible but incorrect draft:
  # it forgets that the input is in nanomolar, i.e. the factor 1e-9.)
  -log10(as.numeric(value_nm))
}

test_pactivity <- function(fn) {
  checks <- data.frame(label = c("1 nM -> 9.00", "25 nM -> 7.60", "2500 nM -> 5.60",
                                 "100000 nM -> 4.00"),
                       c_nM = c(1, 25, 2500, 1e5), expected = c(9.00, 7.60, 5.60, 4.00))
  checks$got <- round(vapply(checks$c_nM, function(x) as.numeric(fn(x)), numeric(1)), 2)
  checks$result <- ifelse(abs(checks$got - checks$expected) < 0.005, "PASS", "FAIL")
  checks[, c("label", "got", "expected", "result")]
}

cat("draft function:\n"); print(knitr::kable(test_pactivity(pactivity_draft), row.names = FALSE,
                                             format = "simple"))
## draft function:
## 
## 
## label                 got   expected  result 
## ------------------  -----  ---------  -------
## 1 nM -> 9.00          0.0        9.0  FAIL   
## 25 nM -> 7.60        -1.4        7.6  FAIL   
## 2500 nM -> 5.60      -3.4        5.6  FAIL   
## 100000 nM -> 4.00    -5.0        4.0  FAIL
cat("\nthe reviewed and corrected version (from R/activity.R):\n")
## 
## the reviewed and corrected version (from R/activity.R):
print(knitr::kable(test_pactivity(helpers$nm_to_pactivity), row.names = FALSE, format = "simple"))
## 
## 
## label                got   expected  result 
## ------------------  ----  ---------  -------
## 1 nM -> 9.00         9.0        9.0  PASS   
## 25 nM -> 7.60        7.6        7.6  PASS   
## 2500 nM -> 5.60      5.6        5.6  PASS   
## 100000 nM -> 4.00    4.0        4.0  PASS
cat("\nconstant offset of the draft, in log units:",
    round(helpers$nm_to_pactivity(25) - pactivity_draft(25), 3), "\n")
## 
## constant offset of the draft, in log units: 9
cat("correlation between the draft and the correct values on the real column:",
    round(cor(pactivity_draft(work$standard_value), work$pActivity), 6), "\n")
## correlation between the draft and the correct values on the real column: 1

Every anchor case fails by exactly 9.00 log units — a factor of a billion in concentration — and yet the draft is syntactically perfect, commented, and returns numbers in a range (around \(-1.4\) to \(-5\)) that a careless reader might rationalise as “some other convention”. The last printed line is the reason the anchor test exists rather than a sanity plot: the correlation between the draft’s output and the correct values is exactly 1. Had the draft been used on the extract, every compound would have been reported as astronomically weak, the model would still have fitted perfectly, and the error would have surfaced only when someone compared a predicted value with a published one. Constant-offset and unit errors are invisible to correlation-based validation, which is precisely why the anchor test exists. The test took four lines and four numbers you already computed by hand in Section 5.

## The five-step policy as a diagram.
steps <- data.frame(
  x = 1:5,
  name = c("DRAFT", "READ", "TEST", "EXPLAIN", "ATTRIBUTE"),
  note = c("assistant writes\na first version", "you read every line;\ndelete what you\ncannot explain",
           "you write the anchor\ntest, on a case you\nsolved by hand",
           "you can defend it\nwithout the assistant\nopen",
           "README records\nthat it was used,\nand for what"),
  fill = c("#dce8f5", "#f7e7d6", "#f6dcdc", "#f7e7d6", "#dcefdc"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

p <- ggplot(steps) +
  geom_tile(aes(x, 0.5, fill = I(fill)), width = 0.86, height = 1, colour = "grey35",
            linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(x, 0.86, label = name), fontface = "bold", size = 3.0) +
  geom_text(aes(x, 0.38, label = note), size = 2.4) +
  geom_segment(data = steps[1:4, ], aes(x = x + 0.45, xend = x + 0.55, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.07, "cm"), type = "closed"), colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = -0.1, size = 2.8, colour = PAL[["orange"]],
           label = "steps 2-4 are the ones that cannot be delegated") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 5.6)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.25, 1.15)) +
  labs(title = "Responsible use of an AI coding assistant: the group's five steps") +
  theme_void(base_size = 9.5) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10.5))
print(p)

Figure 8. The five-step policy. The outer steps are mechanical; the three inner ones are the work, and cannot be handed to the tool that produced the draft. An operational test before keeping a suggestion: can you state in one sentence what would have to be true of the data for this code to be wrong? If not, you have not read it.

The reason to attribute assistance is not legal caution; a reader of your thesis is entitled to know how the artefact was made, exactly as they are entitled to know which package version computed your descriptors[26].

9. Putting it together

The last analytical chunk of this unit is the whole toolkit in one pass: load the frozen extract, select the usable records, convert to the modelling scale, summarise by group, and produce the figure — with every intermediate count printed, so a reader can audit it.

## A complete miniature pipeline, with its own audit trail.
step <- integer(0)
df <- load_data("rock1_chembl_raw.csv", nrows = 200);           step["loaded"]    <- nrow(df)
df <- df[!is.na(standard_value)];                               step["has value"] <- nrow(df)
df <- df[standard_units == "nM"];                               step["units nM"]  <- nrow(df)
df <- df[standard_relation == "="];                             step["exact (=)"] <- nrow(df)
df[, pActivity := 9 - log10(standard_value)];                   step["converted"] <- nrow(df)

cat("audit trail (records surviving each step):\n")
## audit trail (records surviving each step):
for (k in names(step)) cat(sprintf("   %-12s %4d\n", k, step[[k]]))
##    loaded        200
##    has value     183
##    units nM      183
##    exact (=)     142
##    converted     142
cat("\nby measurement type:\n")
## 
## by measurement type:
print(knitr::kable(df[, .(n = .N, median = round(median(pActivity), 2),
                          min = round(min(pActivity), 2), max = round(max(pActivity), 2)),
                      by = standard_type], format = "simple"))
## 
## 
## standard_type      n   median    min    max
## --------------  ----  -------  -----  -----
## IC50             136     6.98   3.92   8.96
## Ki                 6     6.82   5.85   8.22
med <- median(df$pActivity)
p <- ggplot(df, aes(pActivity, fill = standard_type)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity", colour = "white",
                 linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = med + 0.08, y = Inf, vjust = 1.6, hjust = 0, size = 2.8,
           label = sprintf("median %.2f", med)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")]),
                    labels = paste0(df[, .N, by = standard_type][order(standard_type)]$standard_type,
                                    " (n=", df[, .N, by = standard_type][order(standard_type)]$N, ")")) +
  labs(x = "pActivity  =  9 - log10(IC50 or Ki in nM)   (higher = more potent)",
       y = "records", fill = NULL, title = "The extract on the modelling scale") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(p)

Figure 9. Distribution of pActivity in the extract after the five filtering steps, by measurement type. The audit trail above the figure states how many records each step removed; almost all of the drop is the exclusion of records with a blank unit field and of censored records, not of bad data. The distribution spans roughly four log units — a ten-thousand-fold range in potency — with the median marked. The two measurement types are plotted separately because one histogram would average two different physical quantities, and the legend states each count so a reader can judge how much weight each colour deserves.

Three features of that chunk are the habits this unit exists to install: the pipeline is a sequence of named steps with a count after each one, so no record disappears unexplained; the conversion to the modelling scale is a single vectorised expression whose correctness was established by hand; and the figure states its own sample sizes.

## temporary project removed: TRUE

10. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • What an environment is, why there is one per project, and how to create one with renv, in Colab, or with a container.
  • The atomic-vector model — type, length, attributes — why a matrix is a vector with a dim attribute, and what copy-on-modify guarantees that NumPy’s views do not.
  • Why a vectorised expression beats an interpreter loop by a large factor, why growing a result inside a loop is quadratic, and in which three situations a loop is nevertheless the right answer.
  • The recycling rule, the standardisation idiom it enables (scale() and sweep()), and the signature of the silent bug it causes — a result of the wrong length, with no warning when the lengths are multiples.
  • Why every random operation needs set.seed() immediately before it, and what a seed does and does not guarantee.
  • That R does not align named vectors by name, so alignment is a join you write explicitly.
  • How to find out in four commands what a new table contains, what is missing from it, and what it costs in memory; the partial-matching and dimension-dropping traps of base R indexing; and why fread() and read.csv() disagree about empty fields and factors.
  • The split–apply–combine pattern in both dplyr and data.table, and its SQL equivalent.
  • The conversion \(\mathrm{pActivity} = 9 - \log_{10}(c\,[\mathrm{nM}])\), traced by hand, and why potencies are never analysed on the raw concentration scale.
  • What hidden state is, why knitting in a fresh session removes most of it, and the six rules of document discipline.
  • The rule of two, and the mechanics of promoting a chunk to a script in R/ while proving the analysis did not change.
  • The group’s project template folder by folder, and the single test a reviewer applies to it: delete the derived folders, run one command, get them back.
  • The five-step policy for an AI coding assistant, and why the anchor test — not a correlation — is the step that cannot be delegated.

The ecosystem this unit assembles was built deliberately over three decades, from a language designed for data analysis[1] to a package collection with a shared grammar[2], and the computational notebook now counts among the software artefacts that changed how science is done[27]. This course spends its first three units on working practice because most irreproducibility is procedural rather than statistical: surveyed researchers overwhelmingly report having failed to reproduce another group’s result, and many their own[28], and the published remedies are the mundane ones practised here — record the environment, seed the randomness, script the analysis, keep the raw data immutable[29].

Bridge to Unit 2

This unit built a project folder; Unit 2 puts it under version control, pins the environment with renv, hashes the data and attaches a licence and a DOI, so that the folder becomes something a stranger can reproduce and a reviewer can audit. Unit 3 then fills data/raw/ properly — formats, APIs, identifiers and SQL — and the tidy-data unit reshapes what arrives into the table that every later unit models.

11. Self-assessment

Q1. A colleague sends you an R-Markdown file whose figures do not regenerate on your machine, although no chunk raises an error. Name the three most likely causes, in the order you would check them.

  1. A different package version: check the printed environment chunk — a changed default in dplyr or ggplot2 silently changes output; compare against renv.lock. (2) Hidden state in the original: the document was rendered from a session that already held objects no chunk creates, so it knits for the author and not for you; test with rmarkdown::render() in a fresh session. (3) Unseeded randomness: a split or sample without set.seed() immediately before it gives different numbers every run. All three are diagnosed in minutes if the document prints its environment and seeds explicitly.

Q2. In R, does b <- a copy the vector a? When is memory actually copied, and how does this differ from NumPy?

No: both names refer to one object until one of them is modified, at which point R copies — “copy-on-modify”. The consequence is that you can never change a by writing into b, and a function cannot modify its caller’s data. In NumPy, by contrast, a slice is a view sharing memory, so writing into the slice writes into the parent. R trades memory for safety; the price is that repeatedly writing into a large object inside a loop may copy it repeatedly. The one exception in R is data.table’s :=, which modifies in place by design.

Q3. pred has length 200 and obs has length 100. What does pred - obs return, and does R warn?

It returns a length-200 vector in which obs has been recycled twice, and R does not warn, because 200 is an exact multiple of 100. An RMSE computed from it is a plausible-looking number in which half the comparisons are against the wrong observation. Had the lengths been 200 and 99, R would have recycled anyway and emitted a warning — so the dangerous case is the quiet one. Guard with stopifnot(length(pred) == length(obs)).

Q4. Explain why set.seed(0); rnorm(5) run twice gives the same numbers, while rnorm(5) called twice after a single set.seed(0) does not.

R keeps one global generator whose state is a deterministic function of the seed; setting the seed resets that state, so the next draws repeat. A draw advances the state, so consecutive calls return different numbers — which is what you want for independent replicates. Because the state is global and shared by every function, R code must seed immediately before each stochastic step; re-seeding inside a loop destroys independence and makes every replicate identical, a common bug in hand-written bootstrap code.

Q5. You type df$standard_val and get a column of numbers back. What happened, and why is this dangerous?

$ on a base data.frame performs partial name matching, so the prefix standard_val resolved to standard_value. A typo therefore succeeds silently, and the day someone adds a standard_validity column the expression becomes ambiguous and returns NULL — breaking code that worked for a year. data.table and tibble do not partial-match, which is one reason to prefer them; options(warnPartialMatchDollar = TRUE) makes base R warn.

Q6. When should a text column be converted to a factor, and when does the conversion cost rather than save?

Convert when the number of distinct values is small relative to the number of rows (assay type, units, condition labels), and when you want a defined ordering of levels for models and figures. Do not convert when nearly every value is distinct — a SMILES or an identifier column — because a factor then stores the full level dictionary plus an integer code per row. Check with length(unique(x)) first. The related hazard is reading a numeric column as a factor and calling as.numeric() on it, which returns the level codes rather than the values; use as.numeric(as.character(x)) or, better, read it correctly in the first place.

Q7. An IC50 is reported as 250 nM. Compute the pActivity by hand, then state what a pActivity of 8.0 corresponds to in nanomolar.

pActivity \(= 9 - \log_{10} 250 = 9 - 2.398 = 6.60\). Conversely, pActivity 8.0 means \(\log_{10} c\,[\mathrm{nM}] = 1\), i.e. 10 nM. Useful anchors to memorise: 1 nM = 9, 10 nM = 8, 100 nM = 7, 1 µM = 6, 10 µM = 5.

Q8. Your document selects records below a threshold, and the threshold is defined in a chunk below the selection. It knits without error. Is the result correct?

If it knitted in a fresh session, the selection would have raised “object ‘threshold’ not found” — so if it knitted, the object came from somewhere else: an attached .RData, a global-environment leftover, or a cached chunk. Either way the stored output used a value the top-to-bottom reading does not produce. Delete the cache, restart R, knit again: whatever comes out is the only defensible result, and all parameters belong in one chunk near the top.

Q9. Why does raw data live in a folder that code is forbidden to write to, when a checksum would detect an accidental change anyway?

A checksum detects the change afterwards; the convention prevents it. The deeper reason is that every derived file must be regenerable from the raw data by running code — the test of reproducibility is “delete data/processed/, results/ and figures/, run one command, get them back”. If code may edit the raw folder, the chain from source to result is broken and the test is meaningless.

Q10. Why do .RData, .Rhistory and renv/library/ appear in the template’s .gitignore?

The first two are the saved workspace and command history that an interactive R session writes on exit; committing them ships your hidden state to a collaborator, who then cannot tell which objects the code creates and which were inherited. Configure R not to save the workspace at all. renv/library/ is the project’s package library — thousands of compiled files, platform-specific and large; it is rebuilt from the committed renv.lock with renv::restore(), which is both smaller and verifiable.

Q11. An assistant drafts a function and it reproduces your data perfectly, with a correlation of 1 against the reference column. Is that sufficient evidence to keep it?

No, and Section 8 is the counterexample: a draft that was wrong by a constant 9 log units correlated perfectly with the correct values, because a constant offset does not change a correlation. Only an anchor test — a case whose numerical answer you know independently — catches unit and offset errors. The remaining two steps of the policy also apply: being able to explain the function is what lets you predict where it breaks, and attribution is what lets a reader of your thesis judge the artefact as it was actually made.

Glossary

Atomic vector
R’s basic data structure: a contiguous sequence of values of one storage type, optionally carrying attributes such as names or dim.
Attributes
Metadata attached to an R object; dim turns a vector into a matrix, class determines which methods apply.
Bioactivity record
One measurement of one compound against one target in one assay, with a value, a unit and a relation symbol.
Censored measurement
A value reported with > or < rather than =; the true value lies beyond the tested range.
Copy-on-modify
R’s semantics: assigning an object to a second name shares it, and the first modification makes the copy; a function therefore cannot alter its caller’s data.
data.frame / tibble / data.table
R’s three tables: base R’s list of equal-length columns, the tidyverse variant with stricter defaults, and the large-table variant with a query grammar and modify-in-place semantics.
Environment (project)
An isolated set of package versions bound to one project; managed in R with renv.
Factor
A column type storing each distinct string once as a level plus one integer code per row; cheap for low-cardinality text, destructive if coerced with as.numeric().
Hidden state
Objects or results that depend on an execution order the saved document does not record.
IC50 / Ki / Kd
Concentration-scale potency measurements; smaller means more potent. IC50 is the concentration halving a target’s activity; Ki and Kd are binding constants.
Knit
Running an R-Markdown document end to end in a fresh session to produce its output format; the enforced form of restart-and-run-all.
pActivity
\(-\log_{10}\) of a potency expressed in molar; equals \(9 - \log_{10}(c\,[\mathrm{nM}])\). One unit is one order of magnitude.
Partial matching
Base R’s resolution of a name prefix to a full column name in $; silent, and absent from tibble and data.table.
Recycling
R’s rule for combining vectors of different length by repeating the shorter one; silent when one length is a multiple of the other.
renv
The package that gives a project its own library and records exact versions in renv.lock.
Rule of two
Code used a second time moves from the document to R/.
Seed
The integer that fixes R’s global random state, making a stochastic computation reproducible.
Split-apply-combine
Grouping rows by a key, reducing each group, and assembling the results; group_by() |> summarise() in dplyr, DT[, .(…), by=] in data.table, GROUP BY in SQL.
Vectorisation
Expressing an elementwise computation as one whole-vector operation executed in compiled code rather than as an interpreter loop.
